docs.title: Local LLM Manager
docs.text:
A small web dashboard to run local LLMs on your own machines – an NVIDIA DGX Spark, a Mac with Apple silicon, or any Linux box – from any browser on your network.

  • Recipes save how to start a model server (vLLM, SGLang, llama.cpp, TensorFold or any image / native binary), as a Docker container or a native process. You can also import an existing start script, docker run command or compact JSON/YAML recipe file, and export any recipe the same way.
  • Start, stop, restart or "switch to" a model. Switching stops the other models on that machine and frees memory first.
  • Live status, logs and stats: loading / ready / failed, tokens per second, running requests and KV-cache usage.
  • Schedules start, stop or switch models at set times.

  • Several machines, one dashboard: e.g. a DGX Spark and a Mac Studio side by side.

  • Images and weights on every machine: pull Docker images, download from Hugging Face and copy weights from machine to machine (checked with SHA-256).

docs.title: Where to start
docs.text:
• Quick start

    Install the manager on one machine, log in and start your first model.

  • Several machines

    Add more machines as agents and control them all from one dashboard.

  • How it works

    The idea in pictures: one dashboard, all your machines, models shared between them.

  • Architecture

    For administrators: what talks to what, ports, keys and every step on the network.

Everything else – recipes in detail, agents, schedules, security and configuration – is in the README on GitHub for now.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
How the hub and the agents work together: who talks to whom, what each side stores and decides, and what happens on the network when you start a model, add a machine or copy weights. This page is for administrators; How it works explains the same in pictures, without the technical details.

One app, two modes

The hub and the agents are the same program. DGXM_MODE picks the role: the default hub serves the dashboard and stores everything; agent only runs what a hub asks for and has no database, no dashboard and no scheduler. A hub controls its own machine directly, so a single machine needs no agent.

docs.title: The big picture
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    browser["🌐 Browser / phone<br/>(dashboard)"]
    apps["🧩 Apps using a model<br/>(OpenAI-compatible clients)"]

    subgraph hubhost["Hub machine"]
        hub["<b>Hub</b> :8090<br/>dashboard · REST API · scheduler<br/>recipes · jobs · SQLite"]
        m0[("models")]
        hub -. "runs directly" .-> m0
    end

    subgraph a1host["Machine A (Spark)"]
        a1["<b>Agent</b> :8090<br/>/agent/v1/…"]
        m1[("models<br/>Docker / native")]
        a1 -. "runs" .-> m1
    end

    subgraph a2host["Machine B (Mac)"]
        a2["<b>Agent</b> :8090<br/>/agent/v1/…"]
        m2[("models<br/>Docker / native")]
        a2 -. "runs" .-> m2
    end

    browser == "HTTP Basic auth" ==> hub
    hub == "Bearer agent token" ==> a1
    hub == "Bearer agent token" ==> a2
    a1 <-. "weight copies<br/>(share ticket)" .-> a2
    a2 -. "join request (optional)" .-> hub
    apps -- "model API on the recipe's port,<br/>e.g. machine-a:8100/v1" --> m1
  • Solid lines are the control path. Only the browser talks to the hub, and only the hub talks to the agents' API.
  • Dotted lines are the exceptions: an agent with DGXM_HUB_URL asks the hub to add it, and machines copy weights straight from each other after the hub has arranged it.
  • Model traffic never passes through the manager. Apps call the model server on its own port on the machine that runs it.

docs.title: Inside one process
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    subgraph hubp["Hub process (DGXM_MODE=hub)"]
        direction TB
        ui["Dashboard<br/>(static app.js)"]
        api["REST API /api/…<br/>auth · CSRF · lockout"]
        sched["Scheduler<br/>cron / weekdays / one-shot"]
        mgr["Manager<br/>rules · per-host locks · jobs"]
        db[("SQLite<br/>recipes · hosts · weights<br/>schedules · events · join requests")]
        lex["LocalExecutor"]
        rex["RemoteExecutor<br/>(one per agent host)"]
        ui --> api --> mgr
        sched --> mgr
        mgr <--> db
        mgr --> lex
        mgr --> rex
    end

    subgraph agentp["Agent process (DGXM_MODE=agent)"]
        direction TB
        aapi["Agent API /agent/v1/…<br/>Bearer token"]
        alex["LocalExecutor"]
        tr["Transfers<br/>pull · download · copy"]
        sh["Shares<br/>read-only, ticket"]
        jn["Joiner → hub /api/join<br/>(if DGXM_HUB_URL)"]
        aapi --> alex
        alex --> tr
        alex --> sh
    end

    rex -- "HTTP(S) + token" --> aapi
    lex --> dk["Docker / native processes<br/>on the hub machine"]
    alex --> dk2["Docker / native processes<br/>on the agent machine"]
Part Lives on Does Manager hub Owns the rules: port conflicts, memory check, weights check, what Switch to stops, the activity log, background jobs. Picks an executor per host. LocalExecutor hub and every agent Does the actual work on its own machine: docker run/stop, native processes, logs, health checks, /metrics, transfers and shares. RemoteExecutor hub The same interface as LocalExecutor, but every call becomes a request to an agent's /agent/v1/…. Scheduler hub Fires schedules through the Manager, exactly like a click in the dashboard. Agents have no clock of their own. Database hub Everything persistent. Agents keep only process state files, logs and a checksum cache.

Because the hub's own machine and an agent go through the same executor interface, every feature works the same on a single machine and on many.

docs.title: Who holds which key
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    you(["You"]) -- "DGXM_USER / DGXM_PASSWORD<br/>(HTTP Basic)" --> hub["Hub"]
    hub -- "DGXM_AGENT_TOKEN of that agent<br/>(stored in the hub's DB)" --> agent["Agent"]
    agent -- "share ticket<br/>(one folder, read-only, 6 h)" --> other["Other agent<br/>copying weights"]
    newagent["New agent"] -- "POST /api/join<br/>(no login, only lands in a list)" --> hub
  • The agent token gives full control over models on that machine. Only the hub has it; it is never sent to the browser.
  • A share ticket only allows listing and reading the files below one path, for 6 hours. The copying machine never sees the source's agent token, and no SSH is involved.
  • A join request proves nothing on its own: it only appears under Hosts → Asking to be added until someone compares the join code and approves it.

docs.title: Status: what the 5-second refresh does
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant B as Browser
    participant H as Hub
    participant A as Agent (machine A)
    participant M as Model server on A

    loop every 5 s while the tab is visible
        B->>H: GET /api/recipes
        par one request per host, all hosts at once
            H->>A: POST /agent/v1/statuses (all recipes of A)
            A->>A: docker ps / process state
            A->>M: GET health path (e.g. /health)
            A->>M: GET /metrics (tokens/s, requests, KV cache)
            A-->>H: status + stats per recipe
        end
        H-->>B: recipes with status (offline if a host did not answer)
    end

The hub asks each host once per refresh for all of its recipes, so many recipes on one machine cost one request. A host that does not answer shows its recipes as offline without slowing the others.

docs.title: Starting or switching a model on an agent
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant U as You / Scheduler
    participant H as Hub (Manager)
    participant A as Agent
    participant D as Docker / process on A

    U->>H: Switch to "Qwen 32B" (host A)
    H->>H: take host A's lock
    H->>A: statuses of every recipe on A
    A-->>H: running / stopped
    H->>H: checks: port free? enough memory?<br/>weights path known and present?
    loop every other running model on A
        H->>A: POST /agent/v1/stop
        A->>D: docker stop / end process
    end
    H->>A: POST /agent/v1/drop-caches
    H->>H: fill {weights} with A's path
    H->>A: POST /agent/v1/start (complete recipe)
    A->>D: docker run … / start process
    A-->>H: started
    H->>H: log event, release lock
    H-->>U: "started"
    Note over H,A: The status refresh then shows<br/>loading → ready once the health check passes.
  • The hub sends the complete recipe with every start, so an agent needs no copy of recipes and a recipe moved to another host just works. {weights} becomes the path on that host.
  • One lock per host: actions on the same machine (dashboard, scheduler, jobs) run one after another; a slow start on machine A (e.g. pulling a large image) does not hold up machine B.

docs.title: Adding a machine that asks to join
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant A as New agent<br/>(DGXM_HUB_URL set)
    participant H as Hub
    participant U as You (dashboard)

    A->>A: join code = from its token, e.g. K7Q2-X9PM<br/>(shown by installer, log, start page)
    loop every 30 s until decided
        A->>H: POST /api/join {name, url, token, version}
        H-->>A: pending
    end
    H->>U: Hosts → "Asking to be added" (with code)
    U->>U: compare the codes on both screens
    U->>H: Codes match – add
    H->>H: create host with the agent's URL + token
    A->>H: POST /api/join
    H-->>A: approved
    loop every 10 min
        A->>H: POST /api/join (current address)
        Note right of H: only the holder of the approved<br/>token can change the address
    end

Rejected machines stay blocked for a week; requests nobody answers expire after an hour.

docs.title: Getting images and weights onto the machines
docs.text:
Pulls and downloads are jobs: the hub starts a task on each machine and then only asks how it is going. The machines do the work themselves, so a hub restart or a closed browser does not interrupt them.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant B as Browser (jobs panel)
    participant H as Hub
    participant A as Agent A
    participant C as Agent B
    participant HF as Hugging Face / registry

    B->>H: POST /api/jobs/pull (image, hosts A + B)
    par
        H->>A: POST /agent/v1/transfers {kind: pull}
        A->>HF: docker pull
    and
        H->>C: POST /agent/v1/transfers {kind: pull}
        C->>HF: docker pull
    end
    loop every 3 s until both are done
        H->>A: GET /agent/v1/transfers/{id}
        A-->>H: output, GB so far
        H->>C: GET /agent/v1/transfers/{id}
        C-->>H: output, GB so far
    end
    B->>H: GET /api/jobs
    H-->>B: progress per host (also after a reload)

docs.title: Copying weights: host to host, like a snowball
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant H as Hub
    participant S as Source (has weights)
    participant T as Target

    H->>S: POST /agent/v1/shares {path}
    S-->>H: share id + ticket (read-only, 6 h)
    H->>T: POST /agent/v1/transfers {kind: copy, source URL, share}
    T->>S: list files (x-share-ticket)
    S-->>T: names, sizes, SHA-256
    par 4 files at a time, 4 MB pieces
        T->>S: GET file (resume from where it stopped)
    end
    T->>T: check SHA-256 of every file
    H->>T: GET /agent/v1/transfers/{id} (GB, MB/s, time left)
    H->>H: register T's path in the Weights tab

Every machine that finishes becomes a source for the next one. With one machine that has the weights and four that need them, the copy takes three rounds instead of four:

flowchart LR
    subgraph r1["Round 1"]
        s1["Spark 1 ✓"] --> t2["Spark 2"]
    end
    subgraph r2["Round 2"]
        s1b["Spark 1 ✓"] --> t3["Spark 3"]
        s2b["Spark 2 ✓"] --> t4["Spark 4"]
    end
    subgraph r3["Round 3"]
        s1c["Spark 1 ✓"] --> t5["Spark 5"]
    end
    r1 --> r2 --> r3

Download on hosts uses the same mechanism: the first ticked machine downloads from Hugging Face, and the others copy from it, so the model comes over the internet only once.

docs.title: Copies of one recipe on several machines
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    save(["You save the original"]) --> orig
    orig["<b>Original</b><br/>Qwen 32B · Spark 1 · port 8100"]
    orig -- "copy_of" --- c2["Copy · Spark 2<br/>✓ in sync"]
    orig -- "copy_of" --- c3["Copy · Spark 3<br/>⟳ differs"]
    orig -- "copy_of" --- c4["Copy · Spark 4<br/>✓ in sync"]
    c2 & c3 & c4 --> job["Restart job on the hub<br/>hosts in parallel"]

When you save the original, the hub offers to update every copy and to restart the running ones. Copies are rows in the hub's database that point at their original (copy_of). They keep their own name, container name, host and pin; everything else follows the original. Restarts after a sync run as a background job: all hosts at the same time, one after another on the same host.

docs.title: Network ports
docs.text:
From To Port Encrypted? Browser hub 8090 (DGXM_PORT) with Tailscale or tailscale serve / a reverse proxy Hub each agent 8090 with Tailscale or an https:// agent URL Agent hub (join only) 8090 as above Agent agent (weight copies) 8090 as above; the copy dialog warns about plain HTTP Apps model server recipe port, e.g. 8100 as the model server provides it

The Hosts tab marks each host 🔒 Tailscale, 🔒 HTTPS or ⚠ plain HTTP. See Several machines → Tailscale for the recommended setup.

docs.title: Configuration reference
docs.text:
Everything is set in the .env file in the install folder (used by install.sh, install-macos.sh, run.sh and Docker Compose). Copy .env.example to .env; the installers do this for you and fill in secrets. Restart the service after changes (sudo systemctl restart local-llm-manager, or rerun the installer).

Values marked agent matter only with DGXM_MODE=agent, hub only in the default hub mode.

docs.title: Dashboard and network
docs.text: Variable Default Description DGXM_HOST 0.0.0.0 Listen address of the dashboard / agent API. tailscale = only this machine's Tailscale IPv4 (resolved at startup; the manager refuses to start when Tailscale is not connected). DGXM_PORT 8090 Listen port. DGXM_USER admin HTTP Basic username for the dashboard. DGXM_PASSWORD (empty) Dashboard password, at least 12 characters (shorter values or change-me refuse to start). Empty = no login: the manager only answers to requests addressed by IP, localhost or a local/Tailscale name - never by an arbitrary Host header. Always set it when other machines can reach the port: the manager can start arbitrary containers. DGXM_PUBLISH_IP (empty = all interfaces) Address model ports are published on: docker run -p <ip>:<port>:… and what {bind_host} expands to in native / host-network commands. tailscale = this machine's Tailscale IPv4. DGXM_HEALTH_HOST DGXM_PUBLISH_IP, else 127.0.0.1 Host the manager probes model health endpoints on (the published port is appended). Set it when models are only reachable under a different address than the probe default.

docs.title: Modes: hub and agent
docs.text: Variable Default Description DGXM_MODE hub hub: dashboard, database and scheduler. agent: no dashboard, no database - only the token-protected agent API, so a hub on another machine runs models here. DGXM_AGENT_TOKEN (empty) The Bearer token a hub must send to this machine's agent API; required in agent mode, at least 32 characters (openssl rand -hex 32). Enter the same value on the hub under Hosts. The token grants full control over this machine - keep it secret.

docs.title: Models and recipes
docs.text: Variable Default Description DGXM_MODEL_DIR ~/models Directories scanned for local model folders and .gguf files (Weights tab: "Found on your hosts" and presence checks). Comma- or whitespace-separated, several allowed, searched up to three levels deep. DGXM_HF_BIN hf, else huggingface-cli Hugging Face CLI used by "Download from Hugging Face" (Weights tab); downloads go into the first DGXM_MODEL_DIR. Gated models need HF_TOKEN in this machine's .env. DGXM_PUBLIC_URL the address the dashboard is opened with Where the other machines reach this hub, e.g. http://spark1:8090 - needed to copy weights from the hub's own machine when you open the dashboard as localhost. DGXM_HUB_URL – Agent mode: ask this hub to add the machine; approve it under Hosts there when the join codes match. DGXM_AGENT_URL http://<DGXM_HOST or machine name>:<DGXM_PORT> Agent mode: the address the hub should use for this machine when it asks to join. DGXM_AGENT_NAME the machine's name Agent mode: the name it asks to be listed under. DGXM_DOCKER docker Docker binary used to run Docker recipes - e.g. point it at podman where Docker is unavailable. DGXM_DROP_CACHES_IMAGE busybox:latest Image of the throwaway container that drops the page cache (sync; echo 3 > /proc/sys/vm/drop_caches) when the manager itself lacks permission. DGXM_STOP_TIMEOUT 30 Seconds a stop waits for a container / process to shut down cleanly before killing it. DGXM_SEED 1 1 adds two example recipes to an empty database on first start; 0 starts with none.

docs.title: Storage
docs.text: Variable Default Description DGXM_DB ./data/manager.db SQLite database (recipes, hosts, events). Readable by its owner only. DGXM_PROC_DIR <db folder>/processes State and log files of native-process recipes. DGXM_RETENTION_DAYS 90 Days to keep activity-log entries and start-time measurements; pruned on startup. 0 keeps everything.

docs.title: Scheduler and monitoring
docs.text: Variable Default Description DGXM_SCHEDULER_TICK 10 Seconds between scheduler passes (hub). DGXM_ONCE_GRACE_SECONDS 600 Grace period for one-shot schedules ("start once at 06:00") that were missed while the manager was down; older misses are skipped. DGXM_METRICS (off) 1/true/yes serves the manager's own metrics at GET /metrics in Prometheus format (uptime, request and action counts, stored recipes/hosts - no recipe or host data). GET /healthz is always available and needs no login.

docs.title: Secrets passed to recipes (no DGXM_ prefix)
docs.text:
A recipe's environment lists secret names only (one per line, e.g. HF_TOKEN, TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN, EINFACHLLM_API_KEY). At start the manager looks each name up in its own environment - which comes from the .env file - and passes the value into the container or native process. Values therefore never land in a recipe, the database or the dashboard; an agent card shows ✓/✗ per name for the host it runs on.

# .env on the manager's host
HF_TOKEN=hf_…                        # used by recipes that list the bare name HF_TOKEN
TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN=123456:ABC…       # used by the Hermes gateway recipe, for example

Any variable name works: put the value in .env, list the name in the recipe. HF_TOKEN is the canonical example (Hugging Face downloads); see examples/hermes-agent for a real setup.

Note for containers talking to models on the host: 127.0.0.1 inside a container is the container itself. Agent recipes that call a model on the manager's host need http://host.docker.internal:<port>/v1 (or the bridge gateway 172.17.0.1) - and what the program's own config file says wins over variables passed in here (for Hermes: model.base_url in ~/.hermes/config.yaml).

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• .env.example - the starter file with the few keys that matter on first install.
  • examples/hermes-agent - LLM + agent recipes with passed-through secrets.
  • OpenAPI docs of the JSON API: http://<machine>:8090/docs.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text: Local LLM Manager is a remote control for the AI models on your own computers. You open one web page, and from there you start, stop and switch models on every machine you have.

docs.title: The idea in one picture
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    you["👩‍💻 <b>You</b><br/>laptop or phone"]
    dash["🎛️ <b>Dashboard</b><br/>one web page for everything"]
    subgraph machines["Your machines"]
        direction LR
        m1["🖥️ DGX Spark<br/>runs Qwen"]
        m2["🍎 Mac Studio<br/>runs Llama"]
        m3["🖥️ Second Spark<br/>runs Mistral"]
    end
    apps["💬 <b>Your apps</b><br/>chat, coding tools, …"]

    you --> dash
    dash == "start · stop · switch" ==> machines
    apps -. "talk to the models directly" .-> machines

    classDef person fill:#f59e0b40,stroke:#d97706
    classDef hub fill:#6366f140,stroke:#6366f1
    classDef machine fill:#22c55e38,stroke:#16a34a
    classDef app fill:#ec489938,stroke:#db2777
    class you person
    class dash hub
    class m1,m2,m3 machine
    class apps app
  • The dashboard is the one place where you control everything. It runs on one of your machines (the hub).
  • Every other machine has a small helper installed (an agent) that does what the dashboard asks.
  • Your apps talk to the models directly. The dashboard only switches models on and off. It never sees your chats.

Only one machine?

Then the dashboard and the models live on the same computer. You don't need anything else.

docs.title: Recipes: one card per model
docs.text:
A recipe is a saved start button for one model. You set it up once; after that, starting the model is one click. Every recipe is made of three things:

flowchart LR
    w["📦 <b>The model</b><br/>e.g. Qwen 32B"]
    e["⚙️ <b>The engine</b><br/>e.g. vLLM"]
    h["🖥️ <b>The machine</b><br/>e.g. DGX Spark"]
    r(["🃏 <b>Recipe card</b><br/>Qwen 32B on the Spark<br/>▶️ Start"])
    w --> r
    e --> r
    h --> r

    classDef part fill:#6366f126,stroke:#6366f1
    classDef card fill:#22c55e38,stroke:#16a34a
    class w,e,h part
    class r card

You will soon have many recipes: one model in two sizes, the same model on several machines, a fast model for coding and a big one for hard questions. That is fine. Each card is independent, and Switch to makes sure only the right ones run.

Keep the list tidy

Pin the recipes you use daily, give cards a colour or tags (e.g. coding, chat), and use the host filter at the top to see one machine at a time.

docs.title: Which engine should I pick?
docs.text:
The engine (called framework in the recipe) is the program that runs the model. Several exist because they suit different machines and model files. You don't need to know them all, just use the first row that fits:

Your situation Pick Why 🍎 A Mac with Apple silicon MLX Made for Apple chips 📄 The model is one .gguf file llama.cpp Small and simple, made for GGUF 👥 Several people or tools use the model at once vLLM (or SGLang) Fastest with many users at the same time 👤 Just you, on a Linux / NVIDIA machine vLLM or llama.cpp Both are fine

Everything else (TensorFold, Custom) is for special cases: a program not in the list, or a start script you already have. 📋 Import turns such a script into a recipe for you.

docs.title: The easy way: copy what already works
docs.text:
You rarely fill in a recipe by hand. ⚡ Quick recipe takes a recipe that already runs and swaps in another model. Everything else (engine, settings, port) stays the same:

flowchart LR
    a["✅ A recipe that works<br/>Qwen 32B · vLLM"]
    b["📦 Another model<br/>Llama 70B"]
    c(["🃏 New recipe<br/>Llama 70B · vLLM<br/>same settings"])
    a -- "settings" --> c
    b -- "model" --> c

    classDef old fill:#6366f126,stroke:#6366f1
    classDef new fill:#22c55e38,stroke:#16a34a
    class a,b old
    class c new

On the same machine, the new recipe even gets the same port, so your apps don't need any change: just Switch to the other model.

docs.title: Switching to another model
docs.text:
Most machines only have memory for one big model at a time. Switch to takes care of everything in one click:

flowchart LR
    a(["👆 <b>Switch to</b>"]) --> b["⏹️ Stop the others<br/>and free memory"]
    b --> c["▶️ Start<br/>the new model"]
    c --> f(["✅ Ready"])

    classDef step fill:#6366f126,stroke:#6366f1
    classDef go fill:#f59e0b40,stroke:#d97706
    classDef done fill:#22c55e38,stroke:#16a34a
    class b,c step
    class a go
    class f done

The card shows each step live. When it turns Ready, your apps can use the new model. You can close the browser at any point: the machine carries on by itself.

Let it happen on a schedule

Coding model during the day, a big reasoning model at night: under Schedules the dashboard switches for you at set times, even when nobody has it open.

docs.title: Adding a new machine
docs.text:
• 1️⃣ Install

    Install the manager on the new machine and tell it where the dashboard is.

  • 2️⃣ Compare the code

    The machine shows a short code, e.g. K7Q2-X9PM. The dashboard shows a code too.

  • 3️⃣ Add it

    Same code on both? Click Codes match – add. Done ✅

The code works like the pairing code of a Bluetooth headset. If the two codes are the same, it is really your machine. If they differ, click Reject. The step by step guide is in Several machines.

docs.title: Getting a model onto every machine
docs.text:
Models are big: often 20 to 200 GB. The manager downloads a model from the internet once, and then the machines pass it on to each other over your own network, which is much faster.

flowchart LR
    net["☁️ Hugging Face<br/>(internet)"]
    s1["🖥️ Spark 1"]
    s2["🖥️ Spark 2"]
    s3["🖥️ Spark 3"]
    s4["🖥️ Spark 4"]
    s5["🖥️ Spark 5"]

    net == "download once" ==> s1
    s1 -- "copy" --> s2
    s1 -- "copy" --> s3
    s2 -- "copy" --> s4
    s1 -- "copy" --> s5

    classDef cloud fill:#f59e0b40,stroke:#d97706
    classDef machine fill:#22c55e38,stroke:#16a34a
    class net cloud
    class s1,s2,s3,s4,s5 machine

Like a snowball, every machine that is finished helps the next one. Five machines are done in three rounds instead of five. Every file is checked on arrival, an interrupted copy continues where it stopped, and a progress panel shows how long it will take.

docs.title: One setup for the whole team
docs.text:
Example: everyone on the team has their own DGX Spark. Set the model up once and roll it out:

flowchart TB
    o["⭐ Your setup<br/>Qwen 32B"]
    c1["👤 Anna's Spark<br/>✓ up to date"]
    c2["👤 Ben's Spark<br/>✓ up to date"]
    c3["👤 Chris's Spark<br/>⟳ needs update"]
    o --> c1 & c2 & c3

    classDef main fill:#f59e0b40,stroke:#d97706
    classDef ok fill:#22c55e38,stroke:#16a34a
    classDef todo fill:#f9731640,stroke:#ea580c
    class o main
    class c1,c2 ok
    class c3 todo

Everyone gets the same model at the same address. If you change the original later (a newer version, other settings), the dashboard offers to update all copies and restart them.

docs.title: Is it safe?
docs.text:
• 🏠 Stays at home

    Everything runs on your own machines. Your prompts and answers never leave them.

  • 🔑 Password protected

    The dashboard needs a password. Machines only obey the dashboard they were added to.

  • 🔒 Private network

    With Tailscale all traffic is encrypted, and it also works from your phone when you are away.

  • ✅ Checked copies

    Every model file copied between machines is checked, so a broken download cannot start a model.

Want the details?

The Architecture page shows the same things for administrators: which machine talks to which, ports, keys and every step on the network.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text: This page sets up the manager on one machine and starts a first model. For more machines, continue with Several machines afterwards.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Python 3.10 or newer.
  • For Docker recipes: Docker, usable by your user without sudo, with the NVIDIA container runtime for GPUs.
  • The model weights and Docker images you want to run, already on the machine.

docs.title: 1. Install
docs.text:
LinuxmacOSDocker Compose

Installs a systemd service that runs as your user.

git clone https://github.com/einfachllm/local-llm-manager.git
cd local-llm-manager
./install.sh

The installer prints a generated password and stores it in .env in this folder.

Installs a launchd agent. Docker on a Mac cannot use the GPU, so use native recipes (framework Custom (native)) with e.g. MLX (pip install mlx-lm) or llama.cpp (brew install llama.cpp). For importing start scripts, also run brew install bash.

git clone https://github.com/einfachllm/local-llm-manager.git
cd local-llm-manager
./install-macos.sh

The installer prints a generated password and stores it in .env.

Linux only, and only for Docker recipes. Uses the image ghcr.io/einfachllm/local-llm-manager:latest (amd64 and arm64).

git clone https://github.com/einfachllm/local-llm-manager.git
cd local-llm-manager
cp .env.example .env

Set DGXM_PASSWORD in .env (at least 12 characters, e.g. from openssl rand -base64 18), then:

docker compose up -d

Add --build to build the image yourself.

docs.title: 2. Log in
docs.text:
Open http://<machine>:8090 in a browser and log in as admin with the password from the installer (or the one you set in .env).

To change the password, edit DGXM_PASSWORD in .env (at least 12 characters, no well-known passwords) and restart the service.

docs.title: 3. Start your first model
docs.text:
1. Click ＋ Add recipe (shortcut i).

  2. Paste a YAML recipe or a shell script / docker run command - or click YAML recipe or shell script under the box for an example to edit. A YAML recipe only lists what differs from the engine's defaults:

    name: qwen3-8b
framework: vllm          # vllm, sglang, llamacpp, mlx, …
model: Qwen/Qwen3-8B     # a Hugging Face id, or  weights: <name in the Weights tab>
port: 8101

    Scripts are checked for risky calls first; nothing in them is executed. 3. Import, check the fields and the command preview, then Save. 4. Click Start on the new card. The status goes from starting to loading to ready.

A second model with the same settings: ⧉ Duplicate on the card, then change the model. In the editor, Recipe file… exports a recipe as YAML.

When the model is ready, its OpenAI-compatible API is at the endpoint shown on the card:

curl http://<machine>:<port>/v1/models

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Run models on more than one machine: Several machines.
  • Upgrading, uninstalling, schedules and all settings are described in the README.

docs.title: Recipes
docs.text: Recipes save how to start a model server (vLLM, SGLang, llama.cpp, MLX, TensorFold or any image / native binary) as a Docker container or a native process. You can also import an existing start script, docker run command or compact JSON/YAML recipe file, and export any recipe the same way.

docs.title: Importable example recipes
docs.text:
Ready-made recipes you paste into the manager instead of typing fields: open Recipes → Import, paste a whole file from examples/recipes, review the draft (name, port, paths) and create.

Two formats are accepted:

  • .yaml / .json - compact recipe files. The manager's own fields: image, model, ports, args, env, volumes, docker_args, command, health path, tags. Missing settings come from the framework preset, so only what differs is written down. weights: names a registered Weights-tab entry (its per-host path fills {weights}); omit model: for the usual /model mount, or set it to another path. host_port: is the port on the host (port: is shorthand for it). args, env, volumes and docker_args can be multi-line strings or lists.
  • .sh - starter scripts / docker run commands. The manager checks the script, runs it with bash in a restricted mode and turns the captured docker run into the same fields.

The current examples:

File What it is qwen38-27b.yaml Qwen3.8 27B served by vLLM - a small compact recipe with registered weights. qwen38-flash-next-fp4.yaml Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-FP4 on an NVIDIA DGX Spark (GB10, SM121): b12x image, tuned flags, caches, tool calling. Compact form. nemotron-3.5-super-vl.yaml Nemotron-3.5-Super-VL with a draft model for speculative decoding; both models sit in one registered folder. hermes-agent-docker.yaml A Hermes Agent gateway as an agent recipe: its own port and data volume, no model or GPU.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
• Weights: compact recipes name a registered entry (weights:). Create it in the Weights tab with the folder on each host that runs the recipe, or change the name in the file. If a main model and a draft model share a folder, register that folder once, mount it, and point model: at the subfolder (see nemotron-3.5-super-vl.yaml). Starter scripts mount a concrete folder; download the model there, or point the volume at your copy. The Weights tab finds model folders under DGXM_MODEL_DIR by itself and offers them under "Found on your hosts".
  • Ports: the port in host_port: / port: / --port becomes the recipe's port. Keep it the same across models you want to switch between, and give each --served-model-name a stable short name - then Switch to changes the model and your agents keep the same endpoint http://<host>:<port>/v1.
  • Secrets: files list only bare names (e.g. HF_TOKEN); put the values in the manager's .env (see Configuration).
  • vLLM images: the preset command starts with vllm serve. For vllm/vllm-openai (whose entrypoint already runs vllm serve), the manager drops the duplicate; images with a plain vllm entrypoint keep serve. The preview shows the actual command.
  • Recipes are a starting point: the flags are tuned for the machine they ran on. Check --gpu-memory-utilization, --max-model-len and --max-num-seqs against your GPU's memory.

More of your own? Drop new .yaml / .json files in examples/recipes and add a row to its table - or export one from the editor with Recipe file….

docs.title: Several machines
docs.text:
One installation is the hub: it serves the dashboard and stores recipes, schedules and the activity log. Every other machine runs the same app as an agent, which only carries out what the hub tells it to. Only two things go the other way: an agent can ask the hub to add it, and machines copy weights straight from each other once the hub has arranged it. The Architecture page shows all of this as diagrams.

 your browser ──:8090──▶  HUB (dashboard, recipes, schedules)
                           │
                           ├──:8090──▶  AGENT  e.g. Mac Studio
                           └──:8090──▶  AGENT  e.g. second Spark

 apps using a model ──recipe port, e.g. :8100──▶  the machine running it

docs.title: Add a machine
docs.text:
1. Install the manager on the new machine as in the Quick start.

  2. In that machine's .env, uncomment these two lines and run the installer again. The installer has already filled in a random token of at least 32 characters.

    DGXM_MODE=agent
DGXM_AGENT_TOKEN=3f9c…   # generated

  3. In the hub's dashboard, open Hosts → + Add host. Enter the agent's URL (e.g. http://mac-studio:8090) and the same token.

Or let the machine ask to be added

Instead of step 3, also set DGXM_HUB_URL=http://<hub>:8090 in the new machine's .env and run the installer again. It prints a join code (e.g. K7Q2-X9PM), and the machine appears on the hub under Hosts → Asking to be added with a code. Click Codes match – add only if both codes are the same: another machine announcing the same name has a different code. Rejected machines are blocked for a week; requests nobody answers expire after an hour without news from the machine. The machine shows its code also on its start page (http://<machine>:8090) and in its log. Optional: DGXM_AGENT_URL (how the hub reaches it, default http://<its name>:8090) and DGXM_AGENT_NAME. If its address changes later, the machine tells the hub itself.

The new machine appears in the host strip at the top. Recipes now have a Host field that decides where they run.

Keep versions in sync

Upgrade the hub and all agents to the same version.

docs.title: The same recipe on several machines
docs.text:
E.g. a company where every employee has their own DGX Spark: set the recipe up once, then roll it out.

  1. On the recipe's card click ⇉ (Copy to other hosts) and tick the machines. For each one the dialog checks first whether the weights (Weights tab) and the Docker image are there, and whether another recipe uses the same port.
  2. Copy: every machine gets its own copy, named <recipe> · <host>, with the same settings and port - so every employee has the same endpoint http://<their-spark>:<port>/v1 and the same model name.
  3. Later, edit the original (new image, other flags) and save: the manager offers to update all copies. Running copies are listed and can be restarted right away: the hub restarts them on all machines at the same time, also if you close the browser, and a panel shows the progress per machine. Cards show ✓ in sync or ⟳ differs, with sync to catch up.

Images and weights on every machine:

  • Images: in the Images tab, ⤓ Pull… on an image runs docker pull on the machines you tick, all at once (private registries: docker login on each machine once).
  • Weights from Hugging Face: in the Weights tab, ⬇ Download from Hugging Face…. By default only the first ticked machine downloads; the others then copy from it over your network, so the model comes over the internet once. Needs the hf command there (pip install -U huggingface_hub); gated models need HF_TOKEN in that machine's .env.
  • Weights already on a machine (e.g. from your SSD): ⇉ Copy to other hosts… on the model's row. Machines copy straight from each other - the hub only arranges it - like a snowball: each machine that has the weights serves one copy at a time and every finished machine joins in, so 5 machines are done in 3 rounds. Every file is checked with SHA-256, files a machine already has are skipped, an interrupted copy continues where it stopped, and free disk space is checked first. The jobs panel shows GB, MB/s and the time left per machine.

The machines must reach each other at the addresses in the Hosts tab. To copy from the hub's own machine, open the dashboard by its network name (not localhost) or set DGXM_PUBLIC_URL. Use Tailscale names as addresses so copies are encrypted - the copy dialog warns about hosts reached over plain HTTP.

A copy keeps only its name, container name, host and pin; everything else follows the original. To change one copy for good, unlink it: it becomes a recipe of its own. Deleting the original unlinks its copies.

docs.title: Network access
docs.text:
From To Why Your browser hub, port 8090 The dashboard Hub each agent, port 8090 Start and stop models, status, logs (plain HTTP plus the token) Apps using a model the machine running it, the recipe's port (e.g. 8100) The model's API at http://<machine>:<port>/v1 Agent hub, port 8090 Only with DGXM_HUB_URL: asking to be added, reporting a changed address Agent other agents, port 8090 Copying weights (read-only share with a ticket)

Warning

Keep all of this inside one private network – ideally Tailscale, see below – and never expose these ports to the internet. Traffic between hub and agents, and between agents copying weights, is plain HTTP unless you use Tailscale or HTTPS addresses.

docs.title: Recommended: Tailscale
docs.text:
Tailscale puts all your machines and your phone into one private, encrypted network. The dashboard, the agents and the model APIs are then reachable from anywhere, but only by your own devices, and the hub-to-agent traffic is encrypted.

  1. Install Tailscale on every machine (hub and agents) and on your phone, logged in to the same tailnet.

  2. On every machine, add to its .env and restart the manager:

    DGXM_HOST=tailscale         # the manager listens only on this machine's Tailscale IP
DGXM_PUBLISH_IP=tailscale   # model ports too

  3. Add agents under Hosts → + Add host by their Tailscale name, e.g. http://mac-studio:8090.

  4. On your phone, open http://<hub-name>:8090 and use Add to Home Screen. For HTTPS, run tailscale serve --bg 8090 on the hub and open https://<hub-name>.<tailnet>.ts.net.

tailscale is resolved to the machine's Tailscale IPv4 address at start-up. If Tailscale is not up yet, the service fails and systemd or launchd retries it.

Tip

Keep DGXM_PASSWORD set anyway: your phone's browser visits other sites too.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
• Host shows "not reachable": check that the agent runs – on Linux systemctl status local-llm-manager, its log with journalctl -u local-llm-manager – and that the hub can reach the agent's port 8090.
  • "rejected the agent token": the token under Hosts must equal DGXM_AGENT_TOKEN in the agent's .env.
  • The service does not start after setting the token: agent tokens must be at least 32 characters.
